                                     PROJECT NO. 58482


          LARGE LOAD DEMAND                   §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
          MANAGEMENT SERVICE                  §               OF TEXAS
                                              §


               GOOGLE COMMENTS FOR THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION​


    I.​   Introduction

Google, LLC supports efforts by the Commission to implement demand management programs
like the proposed Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) as a means to maintain
grid reliability in both tough weather and market conditions. Various forms of demand response
are needed for the ERCOT grid to be reliable and the ERCOT market to be effective and
efficient over the long term.

One issue not addressed directly in the proposed rule or the Commission’s questions is where
LLDMS should sit within ERCOT’s existing hierarchy of reliability tools. ERCOT already relies on
Non-Spin, ECRS, ERS, and, under SB 6, emergency curtailment authority that may require
large loads to reduce consumption without compensation. Google recommends that the
Commission convene a workshop to examine how these tools should work together, including
the applicable triggers, sequencing, and circumstances under which each should be used. The
objective should be to provide large loads with a predictable framework that allows them, where
practicable, to organize industrial and other operations around a known reliability event and
voluntarily reduce demand before ERCOT must resort to involuntary curtailment or other more
severe emergency actions.

Even without a broader workshop to determine the full suite of emergency operations, the
Commission should better capture the shape of the LLDMS program including the duration,
frequency, and magnitude of response that ERCOT expects to need. Greater clarity on those
parameters would help inform key design decisions, including procurement timing, deployment
sequencing, compensation, and the appropriate budget for the program.

​
​
  II.​   Commission Questions

1. Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not
ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated
some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer’s availability to
reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate
payment to the large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation
period?

Google recommends removing the proposed payment of 25% of the market clearing price to
LLDMS participants that are notified to prepare for deployment but are ultimately not deployed.

Google recognizes that a large load may incur real costs after receiving the 24-hour notice
required under proposed subsection (e)(1). A customer may need to alter production schedules,
staffing, maintenance activities, computing workloads, or other operations in order to ensure that
the committed load reduction is available if called upon. However, those costs are not
necessarily related to the market clearing price for deployed load reduction. An automatic
payment equal to 25% of the clearing price could therefore overcompensate participants and
could materially increase program costs without any corresponding load reduction, particularly
because a single marginal offer establishes the clearing price for all procured participants. If
experience demonstrates that compensation is necessary for identifiable costs incurred in
preparing for deployment, ERCOT could develop a more narrowly tailored deployment payment
methodology through the stakeholder process.



2. Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar
year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

Google requests that the Commission identify the basis for the proposed $54 million annual
maximum. In particular, it would be helpful to understand the assumptions regarding the
expected frequency of LLDMS procurements, MW quantity, obligation period duration,
availability payments, and clearing prices that produced the $54 million figure. The same dollar
amount has been used for Firm Fuel Supply Service, but it is not clear whether that figure was
intentionally used as a benchmark for LLDMS or independently derived based on the
characteristics of this service.

ERS provides a useful comparison. The Commission permits up to $75 million of ERS
expenditures annually, while ERCOT adjusts the amount actually procured based on reliability
needs. A similar approach for LLDMS could provide sufficient spending authority for an
unusually severe year without requiring ERCOT to spend the full authorized amount in years
when the reliability need is lower.
 Google recommends that the Commission consider the annual LLDMS budget together with the
proposed $5,000/MWh offer cap. The two provisions jointly constrain ERCOT's ability to procure
load reductions when they are most valuable from those with capacity to minimize system
scarcity and constraints.

Google takes no position on the proposed $5,000/MWh offer cap; however, we would note that
the economics of load are fundamentally different from energy resources. Previous studies have
estimated the Value of Lost Load (VOLL) for commercial and industrial customers at levels
above $5,000/MWh. Brattle reported the following VOLLs in a 2024 study.1




While Google recognizes the need to protect against unreasonable offers, proposed subsection
(d)(3)(B) already requires ERCOT to reject offers that are unreasonable or outliers. Those
protections allow ERCOT to address potential gaming or market power without preventing it
from procuring load reduction that costs more than $5,000/MWh but remains less costly than
involuntary load shed. Google additionally supports a review of each auction by the IMM to
ensure there is appropriate competition.

The appropriate annual budget should likewise reflect the reliability need LLDMS is intended to
address. Under proposed subsection (d), ERCOT may procure LLDMS only on an as-needed
basis when probabilistic modeling, weather forecasts, or actual system conditions indicate an
elevated risk of an EEA event. Proposed subsection (d)(2) further requires the quantity procured
to be based on a risk assessment informed by probabilistic modeling. EEA events are relatively
rare, and the magnitude and duration of the response needed during any particular event will
vary. Google therefore recommends allowing ERCOT's identified reliability need, rather than a
predetermined annual dollar limit, to drive procurement.




1
 PUC Project No. 55837, Value of Lost Load Study Final Report, Item No. 12 (August 22, 2024), available
at Texas PUC Interchange, https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/55837_12_1421762.PDF
 The EEA thresholds illustrate why flexibility may be important. ERCOT enters EEA Level 1 when
operating reserves fall below 2,500 MW, EEA Level 2 below 2,000 MW, and EEA Level 3 below
1,500 MW. Several hundred megawatts of responsive load may therefore materially affect
whether the system progresses to a more severe EEA level.

However, the duration of the needed response can vary significantly by event. Summer and
shoulder season risk is generally concentrated in a relatively small number of evening hours as
solar production declines while load remains high. Winter risk can extend across multiple
morning and evening peaks during a multi-day extreme weather event.

Accordingly, the appropriate LLDMS procurement cannot be determined in isolation from the
reliability risk it is intended to address or the role LLDMS is expected to play alongside ERCOT’s
other emergency and reliability tools. At the proposed $5,000/MWh offer cap, a $54 million
budget could support 1,000 MW of response for approximately 10.8 hours over the course of a
year. That may provide substantial coverage for several short-duration summer events, but the
same budget could be exhausted quickly during a prolonged winter event requiring sustained or
repeated deployments. The appropriate budget should therefore reflect the anticipated
magnitude, duration, and frequency of the reliability risks ERCOT expects LLDMS to address.



3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how far
in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

Google recommends that ERCOT use a flexible, risk-based procurement cadence that reflects
the seasonal characteristics of EEA risk.

Monthly Outlook for Resource Adequacy (MORA) provides an appropriate early screening tool
because it identifies hourly EEA risk approximately two months in advance. Accordingly, MORA
should be used to identify periods that warrant heightened monitoring, but should not by itself
trigger procurement. ERCOT should increase the frequency of its assessment as an anticipated
event approaches and initiate an LLDMS auction once there is sufficient confidence regarding
the timing, duration, and magnitude of the reliability need.

ERCOT should also retain flexibility to conduct supplemental procurement as forecasts and
system conditions change. This approach would allow ERCOT to target LLDMS to the hours in
which demand reduction provides the greatest reliability value without committing customer
funds too far in advance.

Google recommends distinguishing between procurement of LLDMS and payment for
deployment. ERCOT should be able to procure LLDMS in advance so that participating large
loads are committed and prepared to respond if needed, but the principal payment should be
made only when ERCOT actually deploys the resource.

This structure would allow ERCOT to maintain LLDMS as an available backstop without
incurring substantial costs when anticipated reliability risks do not materialize. Existing, lower
 cost emergency demand response resources, including ERS, should generally be deployed
first, with LLDMS called upon when those resources are insufficient or when additional demand
reduction is necessary to avoid a more severe EEA condition or involuntary firm load shed.



4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

Google does not recommend allowing ERCOT to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies
in this rulemaking.

LLDMS is designed as an emergency resource adequacy tool to help prevent or alleviate EEA
events caused by extreme weather conditions. A transmission emergency is different in nature:
it is generally driven by a localized transmission constraint and may require geographically
specific relief. Expanding LLDMS to address transmission emergencies would therefore change
the purpose of the program, and would also require changing the design to include geographic
considerations in procurement.

If the Commission wishes to consider demand response for transmission emergencies, Google
recommends addressing that issue separately with clear eligibility, locational, compensation,
and cost allocation rules rather than expanding LLDMS beyond its intended resource adequacy
function.

More broadly, Google believes the Commission should provide clear standards governing when
and how LLDMS procurement will be triggered. Wherever practicable, those standards should
rely on objective and transparent triggers – for example, identified probabilities of reaching
specified EEA levels. Google recommends that the Commission establish the governing
principles and minimum safeguards in its rules and direct ERCOT to develop the more detailed
implementation procedures and thresholds through the stakeholder process, subject to
Commission oversight and final approval.

Clear thresholds and procedures are particularly important because emergency actions may
affect not only customers that voluntarily enroll in LLDMS, but also large loads that are not
participating in the program and could nevertheless be ordered to curtail under separate
emergency authority. Greater clarity regarding the conditions, sequencing, notice, and duration
of such actions would give all affected customers a better understanding of their potential
obligations.
 III.​   Comments, Questions, and Suggestions for the PFP Language

In reviewing the proposal for publication language, Google requests feedback on a few of the
provisions:

    1.)​ §25.521(c)(1)(B) - What is the purpose of requiring a price responsive test?​

    2.)​ §25.521(c)(2) - Clarify whether non-overlapping MW may participate in different
         programs. ​
         Is the Commission’s intent to prohibit a large load customer from participating in multiple
         programs altogether, or only to prohibit the same MW of load reduction from being
         committed to more than one program? For example, could a customer separately
         designate non-overlapping portions of its load to LLDMS and another demand response
         or reliability program?​

    3.)​ §25.521(d)(1) - Clarify procurement cadence and triggers. ​
         Google suggests that ERCOT use MORA as an early screening tool, increase
         assessment frequency as an event approaches, and initiate procurement only when
         there is sufficient confidence regarding the timing, duration, and magnitude of the
         reliability need. The methodology and trigger framework should be developed through
         the stakeholder process. ​

    4.)​ §25.521(d)(2) - Require procurement quantities to be based on objective reliability
         criteria. ​
         The quantity procured should be based on objective, transparent criteria developed by
         ERCOT to address the identified reliability need and vetted through the stakeholder
         process. ​

    5.)​ §25.521(d)(3)(B)(v) - Remove the $5,000/MWh cap.​
         A fixed $5,000/MWh cap may prevent ERCOT from procuring economically justified load
         reductions when the value of avoiding involuntary load shed is substantially higher.
         ERCOT should instead rely on transparent standards for rejecting unreasonable or
         outlier offers. ​

    6.)​ §25.521(e) - Clarify where LLDMS sits in the deployment hierarchy. ​
         The proposal does not explain how LLDMS should interact with Non-Spin, ECRS, ERS,
         and SB 6 emergency curtailment authority. Google should recommend a workshop to
         establish sequencing and deployment principles. LLDMS could be procured in advance
         but generally deployed after lower-cost existing demand-response tools such as ERS. ​

    7.)​ §25.521(f)(1)(C) - Remove the automatic 25% of clearing price availability payment. ​
         If customers incur incremental costs after receiving a prepare-to-deploy notice, ERCOT
         should develop a more narrowly tailored deployment payment based on those costs.
    8.)​ §25.521(f)(4) - Base the LLDMS budget on reliability need. ​
        The Commission should identify the assumptions underlying the proposed $54 million
        cap, including expected MW procured, frequency and duration of procurement, expected
        clearing prices, and any availability payments. The budget should be based on need.



IV.​   Conclusion

Google appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and looks forward to any further
discussion.



                                   Respectfully submitted,



                                                  Eric Schubert​
                                                  Strategic Negotiator​
                                                  Energy Market Development ​
                                                  Google LLC

            EXECUTIVE SUMMARY FOR GOOGLE COMMENTS FOR THE PFP

Google supports development of a Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) as an
additional voluntary tool to help ERCOT avoid or alleviate emergency conditions. However, the
proposed rule would benefit from greater clarity regarding the role LLDMS is intended to play
within ERCOT’s broader suite of reliability and emergency tools. Google recommends that the
Commission convene a workshop to examine how these programs and authorities should work
together, including their triggers, sequencing, compensation, and interaction with mandatory
curtailment.

Even without a broader workshop, the Commission should better define the expected shape of
the LLDMS program, including the anticipated frequency, duration, and magnitude of response
ERCOT expects to need. Those parameters should inform procurement timing, deployment
sequencing, compensation, and the appropriate annual budget.

Google recommends the following changes and clarifications:

   ●​ Use objective, transparent procurement criteria. MORA should serve as an early
      screening tool, with ERCOT increasing the frequency of its assessment as an event
      approaches. Procurement should occur only when ERCOT has sufficient confidence
      regarding the timing, duration, and magnitude of the reliability need.
   ●​ Base the quantity procured on identified reliability need. Proposed §25.521(d)(2)
      should require procurement quantities to be based on objective, transparent criteria
      developed by ERCOT and vetted through the stakeholder process.
   ●​ Remove the $5,000/MWh offer cap. Previous studies indicate that the Value of Lost
      Load for commercial and industrial customers may substantially exceed $5,000/MWh.
      ERCOT should instead rely on transparent standards for rejecting unreasonable or
      outlier offers while retaining the ability to procure load reduction when its cost remains
      below the value of avoiding involuntary load shed.
   ●​ Remove the automatic 25% availability payment. A customer may incur incremental
      costs after receiving notice to prepare for deployment, but those costs are not
      necessarily related to the market clearing price.
   ●​ Base the annual budget on the reliability need LLDMS is intended to address. The
      Commission should identify the basis for the proposed $54 million annual maximum. The
      appropriate budget cannot be determined in isolation from the magnitude, duration, and
      frequency of the risks LLDMS is expected to address or from its role alongside other
      emergency and reliability tools.
   ●​ Do not expand LLDMS to transmission emergencies. LLDMS should remain focused
      on system-wide resource adequacy and EEA risk.
   ●​ Clarify whether non-overlapping MW may participate in different programs.
      Customers should be permitted to separately designate non-overlapping portions of their
      load to LLDMS and other eligible demand response or reliability programs.

   •   Remove the $5,000/MWh offer cap. Previous studies indicate that the Value of Lost
       Load for commercial and industrial customers may substantially exceed $5,000/MWh.
       ERCOT should instead rely on transparent standards for rejecting unreasonable or
       outlier offers while retaining the ability to procure load reduction when its cost remains
       below the value of avoiding involuntary load shed.
   •   Remove the automatic 25% availability payment. A customer may incur incremental
       costs after receiving notice to prepare for deployment, but those costs are not
       necessarily related to the market clearing price.
   •   Base the annual budget on the reliability need LLDMS is intended to address. The
       Commission should identify the basis for the proposed $54 million annual maximum. The
       appropriate budget cannot be determined in isolation from the magnitude, duration, and
       frequency of the risks LLDMS is expected to address or from its role alongside other
       emergency and reliability tools.
   •   Do not expand LLDMS to transmission emergencies. LLDMS should remain focused
       on system-wide resource adequacy and EEA risk.
   •   Clarify whether non-overlapping MW may participate in different programs.
       Customers should be permitted to separately designate non-overlapping portions of their
       load to LLDMS and other eligible demand response or reliability programs.
